artiest/dillon-francis.text:
Dillon Francis is an American electronic producer and DJ, born in 1987 in Los Angeles. He played a key role in popularising moombahton and later developed the heavier variants moombahcore and EDM trap. He took an art course at high school, enrolled briefly at Santa Monica College and then switched to a musical career.

His breakthrough came when Diplo noticed him. That led to the collaboration Que Que with Maluca. His track Masta Blasta was a house track at 130 bpm, which he reworked into moombahton, inspired by the Dutch DJ Munchi. In February 2012 he became the first moombahton artist to top the Beatport releases chart, with the EP Something, Something, Awesome. That year he toured North America and supported Nero and Flux Pavilion. In 2013 the Wurld Turr tour of the United States and Canada followed. His debut album Money Sucks, Friends Rule appeared in 2014, followed later by Wut Wut in 2018, Magic is Real in 2019 and Happy Machine in 2021.

Francis shows how a new dance style could find a large audience via clubs and festivals.
artiest/dillon-francis.listen: Listen to Que Que with Maluca. Pay attention to the rhythm: how does the tempo differ from that of ordinary house?

artiest/dillon-francis-en-diplo.text:
Dillon Francis was born in 1987 in Los Angeles and is an American producer and DJ. He took an art course, briefly attended Santa Monica College and then left for Atlanta with five hundred dollars, where he worked on music with a friend. After that he returned to Los Angeles to concentrate on DJing. He played a key role in the rise of moombahton and later developed heavier variants, moombahcore and EDM trap.

The breakthrough came when the American producer Diplo noticed him. Together they made Que Que, with vocals by Maluca. His own track Masta Blasta was first a house track at 130 bpm and was reworked into moombahton, inspired by the Dutch DJ Munchi. In 2010 he released the EP Swashbuckler on Play Me Records. In February 2012 he became the first moombahton artist to top the Beatport releases chart, with the EP Something, Something, Awesome. That year he toured North America. He played at major festivals such as Coachella, Ultra and Electric Daisy Carnival, and with Kill the Noise formed the comic duo Meowski666.

Moombahton is a dance style that slows the tempos of house to the rhythm of Latin American dance music. Dillon Francis showed that such a local scene could seep into the whole of electronic dance music in a short time. He also worked with Diplo, one of the best-known names in DJ culture.
artiest/dillon-francis-en-diplo.listen: Listen to Que Que and notice the danceable, slightly slowed-down beat and Maluca's voice, which talks and sings over the rhythms. How does the song hold the tension without raising the speed?

artiest/dimitri-tiomkin.text: Dimitri Tiomkin was born in 1894 in the Russian Empire and studied at the St Petersburg conservatoire, with Alexander Glazunov among others. He appeared as a concert pianist in Europe and came to Hollywood by way of Broadway. For Frank Capra he wrote Lost Horizon (1937) and It's a Wonderful Life (1946). He made his greatest mark on the western. In High Noon (1952) he used a simple song, sung by Tex Ritter, as a thread running through the whole film. That song became a hit and won an Oscar, as did the score. After that, a title song in westerns became almost a matter of course, as in Rio Bravo (1959) and The Alamo (1960). Tiomkin won four Oscars in total.
artiest/dimitri-tiomkin.listen: Follow the title song: hear how the melody keeps returning in the orchestra, sometimes as a threat, sometimes as nostalgia.

artiest/dimitrie-cantemir.text:
Dimitrie Cantemir was a Moldavian prince, statesman and scholar, born in 1673 in Silişteni in Moldavia. He received a thorough education and learned Greek and Latin as a child. Between 1687 and 1710 he stayed largely as a hostage or envoy in Constantinople, where he learned Turkish, studied Ottoman history and composed Ottoman music. In 1693 he briefly became prince of Moldavia. In 1710 he became prince again, concluded a secret treaty with Russia and fought alongside Peter the Great against the Turks. That war failed, and Cantemir fled to Russia, where he became a prince. He died in 1723.

He is important for music history because he devised a notation of his own, based on the Ottoman Turkish alphabet. With it he recorded 350 traditional instrumental pieces in his work Edvar-i Musiki, a book that he presented to Sultan Ahmed III around 1703 or 1704. He wrote about forty Ottoman compositions of his own, a few of which are still played as part of the Turkish repertoire.

Later ensembles have recorded his music on historical instruments. In 1999 the ensemble Bezmara recorded Yitik Sesin Peşinde, and in 2009 seven of his compositions appeared on Istanbul by Hespèrion XXI. Cantemir shows how old Ottoman music, which was long handed down only by playing, was preserved thanks to a single scholar.
artiest/dimitrie-cantemir.listen: Listen to a recording of Cantemir's compositions, for example by Hespèrion XXI on Istanbul. Notice how different the melody and the scale sound from West European music of the same period.

artiest/dinah-washington.text:
Dinah Washington was born Ruth Lee Jones in 1924 in Tuscaloosa, Alabama, and grew up in Chicago. As a child she played piano in the choir of St. Luke's Baptist Church, sang gospel and became a member of the Sallie Martin Gospel Singers. At fifteen she won a talent contest and began performing in clubs. A club owner was so impressed by her singing that the way to a career lay open, and around 1943 she began singing with Lionel Hampton's band.

Her first record was Evil Gal Blues for the label Keynote, written by Leonard Feather and accompanied by musicians from Hampton's band. Both that record and its successor Salty Papa Blues reached the Billboard Harlem Hit Parade in 1944. After that she became one of the most popular Black female singers of the 1950s. She sang mainly jazz, but also blues, r&b and traditional pop songs. She called herself the Queen of the Blues, and was also known as the Queen of the Jukeboxes. Her 1959 recording of What a Diff'rence a Day Makes is one of her best known.

Washington had a clear, piercing voice with a feeling for the blues and very distinct diction. She died in 1963, aged 39. Her way of singing, in which gospel, jazz and pop come together, was later taken up by many female singers. In 1986 she was inducted into the Alabama Jazz Hall of Fame.
artiest/dinah-washington.listen: Listen to What a Diff'rence a Day Makes and notice Washington's clear diction and how she colours the words with small nuances in her voice. What part does the orchestra play?

artiest/dionne-warwick.text:
Dionne Warwick is an American singer, actress and television presenter, born in 1940 in East Orange, New Jersey. She grew up in a musical gospel family and as a teenager sang in the group The Gospelaires, an offshoot of the Drinkard Singers of her mother and aunt. In 1962 she began her solo career with the songwriters Burt Bacharach and Hal David, and that became one of the best-known collaborations in pop history. Albums from that period include Presenting Dionne Warwick in 1963, Anyone Who Had a Heart in 1964 and Here Where There Is Love in 1967.

After a falling-out with Bacharach and David and a poorer period at Warner Bros. Records, her career got going again under Clive Davis at Arista, with hits such as I'll Never Love This Way Again, Heartbreaker and That's What Friends Are For. She is among the forty biggest hitmakers on the US Hot 100 between 1955 and 1999 and ranks second among female artists with the most hits in the rock era. She won six Grammys and received a place in, among others, the Hollywood Walk of Fame and the Grammy Hall of Fame.

Warwick began in gospel and grew into one of the great singers of pop music. Her work with Bacharach and David is a high point of 1960s pop music.
artiest/dionne-warwick.listen: Listen to Anyone Who Had a Heart. Notice how she sings: restrained or exuberant, and what part the orchestra plays.

artiest/diplo.text:
Diplo is the stage name of Thomas Wesley Pentz, an American DJ and producer, born in 1978 in Tupelo, Mississippi. He grew up in Miami, where he came into contact with Miami bass. At the University of Central Florida he became a DJ at a local radio station. Later, in Philadelphia, he threw parties with DJ Low Budget under the name Hooked on Hollertronix. The success of those allowed him to build a studio of his own, The Mausoleum, in Philadelphia. In 2004 his first solo album Florida appeared, with a more reflective sound than his club music.

He became known as the producer of the British artist M.I.A., with whom he also had a relationship. In 2008 he made her breakthrough single Paper Planes. That same year he had success himself with Blow Your Head. In 2011 he formed the electronic group Major Lazer with Switch, which also got an animated series for FXX. He worked with Dillon Francis on Que Que with Maluca. Later he released albums such as MMXX in 2020, Diplo in 2022 and d00mscrvll, Vol. 1 in 2025.

Diplo shows how a DJ and producer could blend styles such as Miami bass and dancehall into pop music.
artiest/diplo.listen: Listen to Paper Planes by M.I.A. Notice how the song is built up and what can be heard between the vocals.

artiest/dire-straits.text:
Dire Straits was formed in London in 1977 by the brothers Mark and David Knopfler, bassist John Illsley and drummer Pick Withers. The brothers were born in Glasgow and grew up in the north-east of England. Mark was still working as an English teacher at the time. With a few hundred pounds they recorded a demo of five songs, including Sultans of Swing. A DJ at BBC Radio London played the song, and shortly afterwards the band had a record deal.

Sultans of Swing, from the debut album Dire Straits (1978), became a top ten hit in England and America. Albums followed such as Communiqué (1979), Making Movies (1980) and Love Over Gold (1982), with songs such as Romeo and Juliet and Private Investigations. The greatest success came with Brothers in Arms (1985), with Money for Nothing and Walk of Life. It was the first album to sell a million copies on CD. The band played at Live Aid in 1985 and stopped for the first time in 1988. After a return with On Every Street (1991) and a last big world tour, the group broke up for good in 1995.

Dire Straits drew influences from country, folk, jazz and the blues rock of J.J. Cale. The bare, restrained sound came out of pub rock. At the centre was the guitar playing of Mark Knopfler, who played with his fingers rather than with a plectrum. Classic Rock called the group the greatest British rock band of the 1980s. In 2018 Dire Straits was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.
artiest/dire-straits.listen: Listen to Sultans of Swing (1978). Notice Mark Knopfler's clear, fast guitar lines, which answer between the lines of the vocal, and the story about an unknown little jazz band playing in a pub to almost nobody.

artiest/dirk-brosse.text: Dirk Brossé, from Ghent, is a composer and conductor. He teaches composition and conducting at the conservatoire in Ghent. He has written more than twenty film scores, often for Flemish films, such as Boerenpsalm (1989) and Koko Flanel. His best-known film work is Daens (1992) by Stijn Coninx, about the priest Adolf Daens and the workers in Aalst. That film was nominated for an Oscar for best non-English-language film. Brossé writes for large symphony orchestra, with broad themes and a romantic sound. Later he also wrote the music for the BBC/HBO series Parade's End (2012). He is also known as a conductor of film concerts, such as Star Wars in Concert.
artiest/dirk-brosse.listen: Notice the broad, romantic orchestral themes with brass and strings, which give the social drama a heroic colour.

artiest/dirty-three.text:
Dirty Three is an Australian instrumental rock band, formed in 1992 in Melbourne by Warren Ellis on violin, Mick Turner on electric guitar and Jim White on drums. All three had previously played in other groups. Ellis had studied classical violin. At the very first performance, on ANZAC Day, 25 April 1992, Ellis attached a guitar pickup to his violin with an elastic band, so that the instrument had a distorted, feedback-laden sound, very different from what one is used to from a violin.

The album Sad & Dangerous came out in November 1994. Together with tours with Sonic Youth, John Cale and Pavement, it led to a contract with Touch and Go Records in Chicago. In 1996 came Horse Stories, which Rolling Stone named one of the three best albums of that year. After that came Ocean Songs in 1998, Whatever You Love, You Are in 2000 and Toward the Low Sun in 2012. One reviewer felt that Whatever You Love, You Are strengthened the connection with the music of John Coltrane. In 2007 the group curated a weekend of the festival All Tomorrow's Parties. In 2024 their ninth studio album, Love Changes Everything, appeared.

Dirty Three shows that a rock group without a singer can tell a great deal. A violin that sounds like a guitar makes the music both rough and lyrical.
artiest/dirty-three.listen: Listen to Ocean Songs. Notice the violin: when does it sound like a classical instrument, and when like an electric guitar?

artiest/disasterpeace.text:
Disasterpeace is the stage name of Richard Vreeland, an American composer and musician. He grew up on Staten Island and learned a great deal from his stepfather, a trained musician and the music director of their church. As a child he was fascinated by drums and drummed along during the band rehearsals in the basement. In his high school years he learned to play the guitar, and around the age of seventeen he began writing music. He became known as a chiptune artist.

Vreeland wrote the music for many computer games, including Fez and Hyper Light Drifter. For Fez he used few of the usual chiptune tricks. He worked with soft synthesizer sounds and reverb to bring the sound closer to the synthesizer music of the 1980s, used little percussion and processed sounds with bitcrushing and wow. He wrote slow pieces with changing tempos that could move along with the player. In 2014 he made the music for the film It Follows by David Robert Mitchell, who was a fan of his work for Fez. With that he stepped into film music, and he afterwards also wrote for Marcel the Shell with Shoes On.

The music of Disasterpeace shows that the sounds of old computer games can grow into mature electronic film music. Game music always had a colour of its own, and Vreeland brought it to the cinema.
artiest/disasterpeace.listen: Listen to Heels and notice the electronic sounds and the menacing atmosphere they create. Which instruments sound like synthesizers, and how does the tension persist?

artiest/disasterpeace-rich-vreeland.text: Disasterpeace is the stage name of Richard Vreeland, from Staten Island in New York. He learned to play the guitar at high school and began composing around the age of seventeen. His stepfather, a trained musician and church musician, was an important influence. He first became known through game music. For Fez (2012) he used soft synthesizer sounds and reverb to get closer to the synthesizer sound of the 1980s, with effects such as bitcrushing and distortion. His music for Hyper Light Drifter (2016) also received a great deal of attention. In film he broke through with the horror film It Follows (2014) by David Robert Mitchell. Later came Under the Silver Lake (2018), Triple Frontier (2019) and Marcel the Shell with Shoes On (2021), among others.
artiest/disasterpeace-rich-vreeland.listen: In It Follows, listen to the harsh, distorted synthesizer chords and the menacing bass pulses, which recall the horror scores of John Carpenter.

artiest/dizzee-rascal.text:
Dizzee Rascal, born Dylan Kwabena Mills in 1984 in Forest Gate, grew up in a single-parent family on a council estate in Bow, in the east of London. His father was Nigerian and died when he was two; his mother is Ghanaian. At school he was so difficult that he was expelled from four schools, and at the fifth he was only allowed to attend music lessons. There he began making music on the school's computer, encouraged by his teacher Joseph Robson.

In 2002 he signed to the independent label XL Recordings. In 2003 his debut album Boy in da Corner appeared, which he produced himself. It received glowing reviews, won the Mercury Prize in 2003 and is often regarded as the best British hip hop album of all time. After that came Showtime in 2004 and Maths + English in 2007. His fifth album, The Fifth, from 2013, sounded more commercial, and in 2017 he returned to his grime roots with Raskit. He worked with, among others, Arctic Monkeys, Calvin Harris and Florence and the Machine.

Dizzee Rascal is regarded as a pioneer of British hip hop and of grime, a raw form of rap from London. His music also contains elements of UK garage, bassline and r&b. He brought British rap to a mass audience and was the first British rapper with international success. Boy in da Corner let people hear that the streets of East London had a sound of their own.
artiest/dizzee-rascal.listen: Listen to I Luv U and notice the angular, abrasive beat and Dizzee's fast, almost hunted voice. Where does the tension lie in this track: in the rhythm or in the words?

artiest/dizzy-gillespie.text: John Birks 'Dizzy' Gillespie grew up in Cheraw, South Carolina. As a young trumpeter he took Roy Eldridge as his example. He played with Cab Calloway and in the jam sessions at Minton's, where he developed bebop with Charlie Parker. Gillespie knew harmony well and explained the new chords to other musicians at the piano. In 1945 he made the records with Parker that fixed the style. After that he led a big band in which, in 1947, he took on the Cuban percussionist Chano Pozo, which set Afro-Cuban jazz in motion. With his puffed-out cheeks and his trumpet bent upwards at an angle he became a recognisable figure and an ambassador of jazz.
artiest/dizzy-gillespie.listen: Follow the trumpet in its highest register: fast, precise and full of surprising turns.

artiest/dizzy-gillespie-big-band.text:
Dizzy Gillespie was an American jazz trumpeter, bandleader, composer and singer, born in 1917 in Cheraw, South Carolina. Together with Charlie Parker he became a central figure in the development of bebop in the 1940s. His large orchestras, from 1947, were the sound with which that new music reached a wide audience, with arrangements by Tadd Dameron, Gil Fuller and George Russell, among others. He had learned his earlier big band work in the orchestras of Edgar Hayes, Teddy Hill, Cab Calloway and Billy Eckstine.

His big band of the late 1940s also included Cuban percussionists, such as Chano Pozo and Sabu Martinez. From that grew an interest in Afro-Cuban jazz. In 1946 he appeared with his big band in the film Jivin' in Be-Bop. In 1956 he organised a band for a tour of the Middle East on behalf of the State Department, which earned him the nickname Ambassador of Jazz. Recordings from those years include On Tour With Dizzy Gillespie and His Big Band 1956 and The New Continent from 1965. His compositions, such as A Night in Tunisia, Groovin' High and Salt Peanuts, sounded very different harmonically and rhythmically from the swing of the time.

Gillespie showed how fast, complex bebop could sound in a large orchestra, and how jazz could connect with Latin American rhythms. Trumpeters such as Miles Davis and Clifford Brown felt his influence.
artiest/dizzy-gillespie-big-band.listen: Listen to A Night in Tunisia. Notice the syncopated bass line and how it carries the whole piece.

artiest/dizzy-gillespie-orchestra.text:
The Dizzy Gillespie Orchestra was the big band of the trumpeter Dizzy Gillespie, one of the founders of bebop. Whereas bebop was usually played in small groups, Gillespie wanted to bring that fast, intricate music to a large orchestra as well. In the second half of the 1940s he led such a big band in New York.

In 1947 Gillespie brought the Cuban conga player Chano Pozo into his orchestra. With that, Afro-Cuban rhythms found their way into jazz. From that collaboration came pieces such as Manteca and Cubana Be, Cubana Bop, which Gillespie made with Pozo and the arranger George Russell. In Cubana Be, Cubana Bop the music rests on a scale instead of a row of chords, and the conga plays alongside the horns of the big band.

This blend of bebop and Cuban rhythms later came to be called Afro-Cuban jazz. With it, Gillespie's orchestra showed that jazz could open itself to music from other parts of the Americas.
artiest/dizzy-gillespie-orchestra.listen: Listen to Cubana Be, Cubana Bop. Notice Chano Pozo's conga alongside the horns, and how the music stays on one scale for a long time instead of constantly changing chord.

artiest/dj-duro.text:
Duro is the stage name under which Sjoerd Janssen made hardstyle in the early years. He was born in 1984 in Eindhoven and, together with his brother Wouter, born in 1982, forms the Dutch dance duo Showtek. The brothers began their musical career in 2001 with techno and in 2003 switched to hardstyle. Wouter then mainly made hard trance under the name Walt, while Sjoerd produced hardstyle as Duro. Just Begun from 2003 thus belongs to the beginning of the Showtek story.

In 2007 the brothers released their first album, Today Is Tomorrow, on their own independent label Dutch Master Works. It entered the Dutch album chart at number sixty-eight. In 2011 they contributed to the album Kiss from the Past by Allure, a project of Tiësto, and in 2012 singles with Tiësto followed, including Hell Yeah! In 2013 they founded the label Skink, which is licensed by Spinnin Records. In 2014 they made the single Bad with Vassy and David Guetta. In 2014 Showtek reached seventeenth place on the list of the hundred best DJs.

In 2023 the duo returned to hardstyle, with a performance at Qlimax, fifteen years after the last time. In 2024 the hardstyle album 360 Blue followed. Duro's career shows how an Eindhoven hardstyle producer grew into an international DJ duo that worked with the biggest names of the dance scene.
artiest/dj-duro.listen: Listen to Just Begun and notice the heavy, penetrating bass and the tight, fast kick drum that are characteristic of hardstyle. How does the track build up tension?

artiest/dj-maphorisa.text:
DJ Maphorisa is the stage name of Themba Sekowe, a South African DJ, producer, singer and songwriter, born in 1987 and raised in Soshanguve. His family is of Tsonga and Lobedu descent, and his brother Myztro is also a DJ and producer. The word Maphorisa means the police in Tsonga.

As a producer he blends house, gqom, amapiano and Afropop. He broke through with hit singles for artists from widely different genres, such as Y-Tjukuta by Uhuru, Ngud' by Kwesta, Lahla by Busiswa, My Name Is by DJ Zinhle, Jezebel by Professor and Suited by Shekinah. In 2018 he released the single Midnight Starring with Moonchild Sanelly, DJ Tira and Busiswa, and received two nominations at the DStv Mzansi Viewers Choice Awards. With Kabza De Small he made Scorpion Kings and The Return of the Scorpion Kings, both from 2019. In 2021 came the album Rumble in the Jungle with Tresor and Kabza De Small, and he released the single Abalele with Kabza De Small and Ami Faku.

Maphorisa is a key figure of the new South African dance music. His work shows how amapiano and gqom from the townships gave African pop music a sound of its own.
artiest/dj-maphorisa.listen: Listen to a track from Scorpion Kings. Notice the rhythm and the roles of the bass and the keys.

artiest/dj-marlboro.text:
DJ Marlboro, born Fernando Luiz Mattos da Matta in 1963, is a Brazilian DJ. He is regarded as one of the founders of funk carioca, a cross between electro, hip hop and Brazilian popular music, which also draws on African musical traditions. His first LP, Funk Brasil from 1989, marks the beginning of the Funk Carioca Movement.

The idea came from the bailes in Rio de Janeiro, the parties where freestyle music was played. The audience could not understand English and therefore made Portuguese versions of the songs themselves, and Marlboro took that over by making Portuguese versions of American songs. He owes his nickname to a remote district of Rio, in the area called Marlboro Country, where he lived. He makes and presents the radio programme Big Mix in Rio. In 2004 he was introduced to a worldwide audience, when the German journalist and label boss Daniel Haaksman founded the label Man Recordings and put him and Edu K forward. Earlier, in 1999, he had already released Valeu Shock.

In this way an American style, by way of Portuguese versions at the bailes of Rio, became a Brazilian movement of its own.
artiest/dj-marlboro.listen: Listen to a track from Funk Brasil. Notice the heavy bass and the Portuguese vocals over the electronic beats.

artiest/dj-pierre.text:
DJ Pierre, born Nathaniel Pierre Jones, is an American DJ and house DJ from Chicago. Together with his friends Spanky, the technical producer, and Herb J, the keyboard player, he formed the group Phuture in the late 1980s. With it arose a sound that became known as acid house: the squealing, squelching sound that came about through experiments with a Roland machine. Spanky and Pierre visited the club Muzic Box of the Chicago DJ Ron Hardy.

The first acid house track the group recorded was Acid Tracks, renamed by Ron Hardy from the original In Your Mind. It lasted more than eleven minutes and had a slow-burning, bass-heavy and deep sound. DJ Pierre afterwards recorded many of the first acid house tracks for Trax Records, under names such as Phuture, Phuture Pfantasy Club and Pierre's Pfantasy Club, together with Felix Da Housecat. Titles included Your Only Friend, The Creator, Got the Bug and Slam. Your Only Friend is about his drug addiction at the time. Later came DJ Pierre's Nervous Tracks in 2007 and Wild Pitch: The Story in 2017, among others.

DJ Pierre is thus regarded as one of the makers of acid house, a style that from Chicago changed the dance music of the 1980s and 1990s.
artiest/dj-pierre.listen: Listen to Acid Tracks. Notice the squelching, squealing bass sound and how long the track goes on.

artiest/dj-premier.text:
DJ Premier, also known as Preemo, is the stage name of Christopher Edward Martin, an American producer and DJ, born in 1966 in Houston and later raised in Prairie View and Brooklyn. At Prairie View A&M University he was the campus DJ. He formed the hip hop duo Gang Starr with the rapper Guru, with whom he released seven albums, and later the duo PRhyme.

Premier produced all the records of Gang Starr and many by the Gang Starr Foundation, a circle of artists around the group. Among them, in the mid-1990s, were Jeru the Damaja, Group Home and Big Shug. For Jeru the Damaja he made the first two albums, The Sun Rises in the East in 1994 and Wrath of the Math in 1996, and he produced and accompanied Group Home's Livin' Proof in 1995. He also worked for AZ, Common, Drake, Eminem, Jay-Z, Kanye West and J. Cole. In 2010 he founded the label Year Round Records. His own records include Beats That Collected Dust in 2008.

Premier is one of the most important producers of the New York hip hop of the 1990s.
artiest/dj-premier.listen: Listen to a track by Jeru the Damaja, for example from The Sun Rises in the East. Notice the beat and which pieces of music have been sampled.

artiest/dj-screw.text:
DJ Screw, born Robert Earl Davis Jr. in 1971, was an American hip hop DJ from Houston, Texas, and the inventor of the chopped-and-screwed technique. He grew up in Smithville, where as a child he wanted to be a driver like his father. The 1984 film Breakin' and his mother's turntable led him to music. He began as a DJ at the age of twelve and from 1990 made his characteristic slowed-down mixes.

That slowed-down style became his most important work in 1991 and 1992. The mixes began as special compilations for friends. Later he put them on sale, and fans from Dallas and Waco queued outside his house in Houston. He started a business of his own, Screwed Up Records and Tapes, and led the group Screwed Up Click. He released more than 350 mixtapes. In 2000 he died of a codeine overdose, aged twenty-nine. A wider audience only discovered his legacy around 2005.

What DJ Screw did is best heard as a sound that has been slowed down. The tempo drops, the voices become deeper and the whole acquires a heavy, dragging atmosphere. Many later artists adopted that style.
artiest/dj-screw.listen: Listen to one of his mixtapes, such as Diary of the Originator: Chapter 354. Notice how the slowed-down tempo and the deep voices change the familiar songs.

artiest/dj-shadow.text:
DJ Shadow is the stage name of Joshua Paul Davis, an American DJ and producer, born in 1972. As a schoolboy in Davis, California, he experimented with a four-track recorder and began as a DJ at the university's student radio station KDVS. He became involved with the British label Mo' Wax, which was known for experimental hip hop. In early 1993 he helped found the underground hip hop label Solesides, together with Blackalicious and Lyrics Born. His first singles, such as In/Flux and Lost and Found (S.F.L.), appeared on Mo' Wax.

His first album, Endtroducing....., came out at the end of 1996 and was very well received. In 2001 it was included in the Guinness World Records book as the first album made entirely from samples. Davis used only an AKAI MPC60 II, a sampling drum machine, two turntables and a borrowed Pro Tools setup. In 1998 he produced Psyence Fiction, the debut of UNKLE, with guests such as Thom Yorke, Richard Ashcroft and Mike D. Around 2000 he wrote the music for the documentary Dark Days, about homeless people living in a subway tunnel. Later came albums such as The Private Press in 2002, The Outsider in 2006 and The Mountain Will Fall in 2016.

DJ Shadow shows that an album made only of samples can tell a story of its own.
artiest/dj-shadow.listen: Listen to a track from Endtroducing..... and try to hear how many different fragments run through one another. Which do you recognise?

artiest/dj-snake.text:
DJ Snake is the stage name of William Sami Étienne Grigahcine, a French producer, born in 1986 in Paris to Algerian parents. He grew up in Ermont, a suburb of the city. As a boy he was influenced by the film La Haine and by hip hop artists such as KRS-One and Cypress Hill. In 2011 he co-produced the album Born This Way by Lady Gaga, which earned him a Grammy nomination for Album of the Year.

He first worked for other artists, including Pitbull with Shut It Down and Lady Gaga with Applause. His breakthrough came in 2013 with his debut single Turn Down for What, with Lil Jon. The song reached number four on the US Hot 100, was nominated for a Grammy for best music video and won a Billboard award in 2015. In 2014 he played as a supporting act, together with Dillon Francis, on Skrillex's Mothership Tour. In 2015 he performed at Coachella. His debut album Encore from 2016 contained Let Me Love You with Justin Bieber, and his second album Carte Blanche from 2019 contained Taki Taki with Selena Gomez, Ozuna and Cardi B. In 2016 Forbes placed him on its 30 Under 30 in Music list.

DJ Snake shows how a French producer from a Paris suburb could make a worldwide dance hit, and how hip hop and electronic music came together in the 2010s.
artiest/dj-snake.listen: Listen to Turn Down for What. Notice the rhythm and which sounds keep returning.

artiest/django-reinhardt.text: Django Reinhardt was born in Belgium into a family of travelling Manouche people and grew up in a caravan camp near Paris. In 1928 he was badly injured in a fire in his caravan; two fingers of his left hand remained paralysed. He developed a two-finger technique for his solos. When he heard records by Louis Armstrong, he knew he wanted to play jazz. With the violinist Stéphane Grappelli he founded the Quintette du Hot Club de France in 1934. He played fast, virtuoso lines with a great feeling for melody, as in his own Nuages. After the war he switched to electric guitar and also played bebop. He died in 1953 of a brain haemorrhage.
artiest/django-reinhardt.listen: Hear how fast and clear the solo guitar plays, with two fingers.

artiest/djivan-gasparyan.text:
Djivan Gasparyan was born in 1928 in Solak in Armenia, to parents from Mush, and died in 2021 at the age of 92. He played the duduk, a wooden double-reed instrument related to the oboe, and was called the Master of the duduk. He began at the age of six. In 1948 he became a soloist with the Armenian Song and Dance Ensemble and with the Yerevan philharmonic orchestra. He won four medals at worldwide UNESCO competitions and in 1978 received the title People's Artist of the Armenian Soviet Republic.

Gasparyan taught as a professor at the Yerevan conservatoire and trained many duduk players. In 1998 he released an album with a duduk quartet of his own, with new alto and bass duduks, which he himself called a particularly difficult undertaking. He worked with many well-known artists, including Sting, Peter Gabriel, Brian May, Brian Eno, Hans Zimmer, Ludovico Einaudi and David Sylvian, and recorded with the Kronos Quartet and the Los Angeles Philharmonic. In 2006 he received a Grammy nomination for best traditional world music album and in 2002 the Lifetime Achievement Award of WOMEX. In 2010 he took part in the Armenian entry at the Eurovision Song Contest.

The sound of the duduk is warm, nasal and plaintive, with a breathing tone that resembles a human voice. Peter Gabriel said that Gasparyan enchanted all listeners the moment he put the duduk to his lips. Through his collaborations the duduk became known worldwide, in film music and in pop music too.
artiest/djivan-gasparyan.listen: Listen to Dle Yaman and notice the warm, breathing tone of the duduk. Can you hear how the melody is sustained for a long time and slowly bends, almost like a singing voice?

artiest/dmitri-hvorostovsky.text:
Dmitri Hvorostovsky was a Russian opera baritone, born in 1962 in Krasnoyarsk in Siberia, a city that was then largely closed to foreigners. He grew up as an only child, largely with his grandparents, because his father, an engineer, and his mother, a gynaecologist, were rarely at home. In 1989 he gained international fame when he won the BBC Cardiff Singer of the World, beating the Welsh favourite Bryn Terfel in the final, with, among other pieces, Ombra mai fu by Handel and an aria from Verdi's Don Carlos.

His opera debut in the West followed in 1989 in Nice, in Tchaikovsky's The Queen of Spades. In Italy he made his name as Eugene Onegin at La Fenice. In 1992 he made his debut at Covent Garden in Bellini's I puritani, in 1993 in Chicago in La traviata and in 1995 at the Metropolitan Opera. He later sang in virtually all the great opera houses, including the Berlin State Opera, La Scala and the Vienna State Opera. His interpretation of Eugene Onegin in particular was acclaimed; The New York Times wrote that he was born for that role. In 2003 he gave a recital at the Kremlin Palace in Moscow with new arrangements of songs from the Second World War, which was watched on Russian television by more than ninety million viewers. In his later years he sang almost only Verdi. He died in 2017 in London of brain cancer.

Hvorostovsky was one of the best-known Russian singers of his generation and brought the Russian singing tradition to the international opera stage.
artiest/dmitri-hvorostovsky.listen: Listen to his performance of an aria from Eugene Onegin. Notice how his baritone voice carries the story.

artiest/dmitri-sjostakovitsj.text: Dmitri Shostakovich studied in Petrograd and became famous at nineteen with his First Symphony. His career was constantly under pressure from the Soviet regime: in 1936 Pravda tore apart his opera Lady Macbeth of the Mtsensk District and he had to fear for his life. He wrote fifteen symphonies and fifteen string quartets full of irony, violence and mourning. His Eighth String Quartet from 1960 revolves around his musical monogram, the notes D-Es-C-H (D, E flat, C, B natural in German notation).
artiest/dmitri-sjostakovitsj.listen: Listen to the beginning of the Eighth String Quartet and hear how the cello alone plays the four notes D-Es-C-H on its own, after which the other instruments take them up one by one.

artiest/dobie-gray.text:
Dobie Gray was born in 1940 in Simonton, Texas, as Lawrence Darrow Brown. His family worked as sharecroppers, and through his grandfather, a Baptist preacher, he became acquainted with gospel. In the early 1960s he moved to Los Angeles to become an actor and sang to earn money. He recorded under various names, until Sonny Bono sent him to the small label Stripe Records. There he was given the name Dobie Gray, a reference to the popular sitcom The Many Loves of Dobie Gillis.

His first small success came in 1962 with the single Look At Me, recorded with the bassist Carol Kaye, which reached number 91 on the Billboard Hot 100. His first album, Look!, did not sell, but in 1965 he became widely known with The 'In' Crowd, written by Billy Page, which reached number 13 in the United States and number 25 in England. Ramsey Lewis and Petula Clark later recorded the song as well. Gray then sang the title song of the 1966 film Out of Sight, the song Out on the Floor, and from 1968 to 1969 was in the cast of the musical Hair in Hollywood. His biggest hit became Drift Away in 1973, a song by Mentor Williams. It sold more than a million copies and can still often be heard on the radio.

Gray's music encompasses soul, country, pop and musical theatre. He died in 2011. His voice, which sounds warm and cheerful, belongs to the soul pop of the 1960s and 1970s.
artiest/dobie-gray.listen: Listen to Out on the Floor and notice the tempo, the danceable accompaniment and Gray's confident voice. Which instruments give the song its drive?

artiest/doc-watson.text:
Arthel Lane Watson, known as Doc Watson, was born in 1923 in Deep Gap, North Carolina. Before his second birthday he lost his sight through an eye infection. As a boy he bought his first guitar with money earned by chopping down dead chestnut trees, and learned songs by the Carter Family, Jimmie Rodgers and the Delmore Brothers. He got his nickname during a live radio broadcast: someone in the audience called out that the presenter should simply call him Doc.

In the 1950s Watson played electric guitar in a country band and translated fiddle tunes to the guitar. In 1960 the folk expert Ralph Rinzler advised him to play only acoustic from then on. His first recording was Old Time Music at Clarence Ashley's, and his 1961 appearance in Greenwich Village brought him to the clubs and universities of the folk revival. His albums from that time included Doc Watson and Southbound. In 1972 he sang Tennessee Stud on the album Will the Circle Be Unbroken. After that he played for years with his son Merle, until Merle was killed in a farm accident in 1985.

Watson played both with a plectrum and with his fingers, but is best known for his flatpicking: fast lead guitar with fiddle tunes and crosspicking. He was also a good banjo player and sang with a warm baritone. Guitarists such as Clarence White and Tony Rice took over his style and built on it. He won seven Grammys and a Lifetime Achievement Award. MerleFest in North Carolina is named after his son. In a history of pop music, Watson shows how old American mountain music came back to life in the folk revival.
artiest/doc-watson.listen: Listen to Tennessee Stud by Doc Watson and notice the fast, clear guitar line that sounds like a fiddle tune. Can you hear how his baritone voice rests calmly on top of it?

artiest/dock-boggs.text:
Moran Lee Dock Boggs was born in 1898 in West Norton, Virginia, the youngest of ten children. When he was born, the railway in the Appalachians had only just arrived, and with mining the family changed from self-sufficient farmers into wage workers in mining towns. His father, a carpenter and blacksmith, loved singing and taught his children to sing. As a child Dock followed a Black guitarist, called Go Lightning, who played along the railway, and he sneaked at night to the Black camps to hear string bands. He became fascinated by picking on the banjo, whereas at home he knew only frailing.

When he went to work in the mine, he played more often and more seriously. His brother Roscoe and the travelling musician Homer Crawford taught him many techniques. From Crawford he had Hustlin' Gambler, the basis of his own Country Blues. In 1927 his recording career began, and two records from the 1920s, Sugar Baby and Country Blues, ended up in 1952 on Harry Smith's Anthology of American Folk Music.

Those recordings made Boggs a key figure for later folk musicians. His banjo playing and singing combine Appalachian folk music with the blues of Black musicians, and that is a mixture of its own. During the folk revival of the 1960s he was rediscovered. He performed at folk festivals and recorded for Folkways Records. He died in 1971, on his seventy-third birthday.
artiest/dock-boggs.listen: Listen to Country Blues and notice the picking on the banjo and the raw, almost speaking singing. Can you hear the blues feeling in an instrument you mainly associate with country music?

artiest/doe-maar.text:
Doe Maar was formed in 1978 by keyboard player and singer Ernst Jansz and bassist Piet Dekker, with guitarist Jan Hendriks and drummer Carel Copier. Jansz and Dekker had previously played together in Boudewijn de Groot's backing band. In 1980 Henny Vrienten joined as bassist and singer. Doe Maar played ska and reggae with Dutch lyrics, and in doing so proved that pop music in Dutch did not have to sound old-fashioned.

The debut album Doe Maar (1979) was poorly received. Skunk (1981) went to number 1 in the album chart. It contains Sinds 1 dag of 2 (32 jaar), about a 32-year-old man who, to his own surprise, is in love again, with the guitar on the offbeat, the beat between the beats. The radio DJ Frits Spits gave the song its title. Most of the songs came from Vrienten and Jansz, and were about being in love, puberty, parents and boredom, in the language in which young people talked to one another. In 1982 the band broke through on a massive scale. The single De bom, about life under the threat of cruise missiles, spent four weeks at number 1 in the Top 40 in December 1982. The album 4us (1983) also reached number 1.

Teenagers followed Doe Maar as their parents had followed The Beatles. In February 1984 the band announced its end, and on 14 April 1984 two farewell concerts followed in the Maaspoort in Den Bosch. After that, Dutch-language bands such as Het Goede Doel, Klein Orkest and the Frank Boeijen Groep got more room. Doe Maar later returned, in 2000 and 2008, among other occasions. Vrienten died in 2022.
artiest/doe-maar.listen: In Sinds 1 dag of 2 (32 jaar) the guitar plays on the offbeat, the beat between the beats, as in Jamaican ska. Listen to how that bouncing rhythm makes the lyrics about a thirty-something in love light and a little mocking.

artiest/doja-cat.text:
Doja Cat is the stage name of Amala Dlamini, an American rapper, singer and songwriter, born in 1995 in Los Angeles. Her father is a South African performer, her mother an American graphic designer. As a child she lived for a few years in an ashram in Agoura Hills, where the jazz musician Alice Coltrane was the spiritual leader. Later she took up breakdancing and popping and locking. At sixteen she left school and taught herself to sing, rap and produce, with beats she found on YouTube.

In 2012 she attracted attention with So High on SoundCloud. In 2014 her first EP Purrr! appeared, and in the same year she signed to Kemosabe and RCA Records. Her debut album Amala from 2018 hardly made a mark, but the absurd Mooo! became an internet meme that year. With Hot Pink in 2019 she broke through, mainly thanks to Say So, which spread at lightning speed via TikTok. After that came the albums Planet Her in 2021 and Scarlet in 2023.

Her music shifts between rap, r&b, pop and dance and changes tone from funny to soft. She raps and sings in the same track and plays with styles, even to the point of a metal version of Say So at an awards show. Doja Cat shows how an artist in the 2020s breaks through via social media and viral clips, before a record company knows its plan.
artiest/doja-cat.listen: Listen to Say So and notice how she switches between singing and rapping. Can you hear the danceable rhythm section under the light voice?

artiest/dolly-parton.text:
Dolly Parton was born in 1946 in a one-room cabin in Pittman Center, Tennessee, the fourth of twelve children in a poor family. She sang on local radio and television as a child, recorded a first single at thirteen and as a young girl moved to Nashville. There she first wrote songs for others, together with her uncle Bill Owens. Her own record contract with Monument Records brought little at first, until she was allowed to sing country. In 1967 her debut album Hello, I'm Dolly appeared.

That year she joined Porter Wagoner's television show. Together they made many duets, and she gradually built a career of her own with Joshua in 1971 and Coat of Many Colors. Her greatest breakthrough of those years was Jolene from 1973. She left Wagoner in 1974 and afterwards wrote I Will Always Love You about their break-up. With Here You Come Again from 1977 she bridged the gap to a pop audience. She also acted in films, including 9 to 5 in 1980, and founded the theme park Dollywood.

Parton wrote more than three thousand songs and won eleven Grammys. Her high, clear soprano and her storytelling lyrics about poverty, love and parting made her one of the most successful women in country music. Many other artists covered her work. She died in 2026.
artiest/dolly-parton.listen: Listen to Jolene and notice the fast, repeated guitar figure with which the song begins. Can you hear how her voice pleads, while the accompaniment stays flat and firm?

artiest/don-cherry.text: The trumpeter Don Cherry grew up in Los Angeles and from 1958 played with Ornette Coleman, who shaped his musical thinking. He played a small pocket trumpet. After Coleman he played with Sonny Rollins and Albert Ayler. On Complete Communion (1965) he made suites in which themes and improvisations merge into one another without a break. After that he moved to Sweden, where he lived with his wife, the artist Moki Cherry. He travelled widely and learned music from India, Africa, Turkey and Brazil. In this way he became one of the first to truly bring world music and jazz together, as on Brown Rice (1975). He died in 1995.
artiest/don-cherry.listen: Hear how the trumpet moves between jazz and melodies from other cultures.

artiest/don-everly.text:
Isaac Donald Everly, Don Everly for short, was born in 1937 in Brownie, Kentucky. His father Ike was a guitarist and taught his sons to play. The family moved to Knoxville, Tennessee, in 1953, and by 1955 Don and his younger brother Phil were living in Nashville. Together they formed the Everly Brothers. Their first performances were already in 1951, and in 1957 they signed to Cadence Records.

Their first hit was Bye Bye Love, a song by Felice and Boudleaux Bryant that had been turned down by thirty other artists. It became their first million-seller. After that came All I Have to Do Is Dream and Cathy's Clown, among others. After conflicts between the brothers the duo broke up. From 1973 to 1983 they made solo work. Don played in Nashville with his band Dead Cowboys and in 1979 sang with Emmylou Harris. In 1983 the brothers stood on stage together again at the Royal Albert Hall in London.

The Everly Brothers sang with tight two-part harmonies, with Don taking the low voice and Phil the high, accompanied by acoustic guitars. Paul McCartney said that he and John Lennon, in their early years, played at being Phil and Don. In 1986 the Everly Brothers were the first duo to be inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame. Don Everly died in 2021.
artiest/don-everly.listen: Listen to Bye Bye Love by the Everly Brothers and notice the two voices that sound almost like one. Can you hear how the guitars carry the rhythm?

artiest/don-redman.text:
Don Redman was born in 1900 in Piedmont, West Virginia. His father was a music teacher, his mother a singer. At three he played the trumpet, and at twelve he had mastered almost all the wind instruments, from trumpet to oboe, and piano as well. After studying at Storer College and the Boston conservatory he moved to New York. In the early 1920s he joined Fletcher Henderson's orchestra, where he mainly played clarinet and saxophone and soon began writing the arrangements.

Those arrangements made him important. Redman set the brass against the reeds: one section played a figure, the other answered. He let the melody move from section to section and from soloist to soloist, and wrote harmonies underneath the solos. In this way he laid the foundation for the sound that would later be called swing, and for much big band music in the decades afterwards. In 1927 he became musical director of McKinney's Cotton Pickers, and in 1931 he started his own orchestra, which played for a long time at Connie's Inn in Manhattan. With Chant of the Weed he had a first hit that year. His records for Brunswick from 1931 to 1934 are among the most intricate jazz arrangements from before the swing era.

After 1940 Redman disbanded his band and wrote arrangements for Jimmy Dorsey, Count Basie and Harry James, among others. In the 1950s he led the band of the singer Pearl Bailey. He died in 1964 in New York. His cousin Dewey Redman and second cousin Joshua Redman also became saxophonists.
artiest/don-redman.listen: In Chant of the Weed by Don Redman and his Orchestra, listen to the different groups of wind instruments. Notice how the melody does not stay with one instrument, but is passed between saxophones, brass and soloists.

artiest/donald-byrd.text: The trumpeter Donald Byrd, from Detroit, came to New York in 1955 and succeeded Clifford Brown in Art Blakey's Jazz Messengers; Brown's playing was his model. He played on many hard bop records for Blue Note. On A New Perspective (1963) he used a gospel choir. Byrd also studied at universities and taught jazz history. In the 1970s he worked with the producers Larry and Fonce Mizell on soul and funk records such as Black Byrd (1973), Blue Note's best-selling album up to then. Purists considered it a betrayal; hip hop producers later sampled his music a great deal. In 1993 he played on Guru's Jazzmatazz.
artiest/donald-byrd.listen: Hear the trumpet above a funky groove with vocals: jazz for the dance floor.

artiest/donald-duck-dunn.text:
Donald Dunn was born in 1941 in Memphis, Tennessee. His father gave him the nickname Duck, after the Disney cartoon duck. As a boy he cycled and played sport with Steve Cropper, and when Cropper took up the guitar, Dunn chose the bass guitar. He taught himself to play by playing along with records. With Cropper and other school friends he formed the Royal Spades, who as the Mar-Keys scored a national hit in 1961 with Last Night on the label Satellite, the later Stax.

In 1965 Dunn became the bassist of Booker T. & the M.G.'s, the house band of Stax. There he played on thousands of records, including by Otis Redding, Sam & Dave, Rufus Thomas and Albert King. His bass lines in Respect and I Can't Turn You Loose by Redding, Hold On, I'm Comin' by Sam & Dave and Born Under a Bad Sign by Albert King became a model for other r&b musicians. They are simple, tight and melodic, and follow no textbook. Dunn played a Fender Precision Bass with thick flatwound strings, which explains his round, warm tone.

Later he worked with Muddy Waters, Eric Clapton, Tom Petty, Stevie Nicks and Neil Young. With Cropper he played in the Blues Brothers Band and appeared in the films The Blues Brothers (1980) and Blues Brothers 2000 (1998), pipe in mouth. Dunn died in 2012 in Tokyo, after a concert with Cropper. His role at Stax shows that the soul of Memphis was made by a band of Black and white musicians together.
artiest/donald-duck-dunn.listen: In Hold On, I'm Comin' by Sam & Dave, listen to Dunn's bass line. Notice how, together with the drums, it pushes the song forward, while the horns and the singers answer above it.

artiest/donald-fagen.text:
Donald Fagen was born on 10 January 1948 in Passaic, New Jersey. He grew up in a new suburb, which he experienced as a prison. His first record was Reelin' and Rockin' by Chuck Berry, but after a visit to the Newport Jazz Festival he became, as he put it himself, a jazz snob. As a teenager he went to concerts by Charles Mingus, Thelonious Monk and Miles Davis in New York. Later he also fell under the spell of soul, funk and Motown.

At Bard College he met Walter Becker in 1967. Together they first worked as songwriters, and in 1970 they started Steely Dan, named after an object from a novel by William S. Burroughs. Fagen sang and played keyboards, and the two wrote all the songs. After 1974 Steely Dan became a studio project in which Becker and Fagen worked with an ever-changing cast of session musicians. Aja (1977) became their best-selling album, followed by Gaucho. After the split in 1981 Fagen made the solo album The Nightfly (1982), inspired by his suburban childhood and his love of late-night radio. Later followed Kamakiriad (1993), Morph the Cat (2006) and Sunken Condos (2012).

Fagen and Becker brought jazz harmonies into the pop song and had their songs played by a changing group of top musicians. In this way the studio became their real instrument. In 2001 Steely Dan was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame. After Becker's death in 2017 Fagen continued to perform under the band name until 2024.
artiest/donald-fagen.listen: Listen to I.G.Y. from The Nightfly (1982). Notice the rich jazz chords beneath a relaxed pop rhythm, and the lyrics, which look back with a wink at the optimistic vision of the future of the late 1950s.

artiest/donald-harrison.text:
Donald Harrison Jr. is an American jazz saxophonist, born in 1960 in New Orleans. His father, Big Chief Donald Harrison Sr., was a leader of the Mardi Gras Indians, and Donald grew up in the culture of the second line and the masked parades. At sixteen he began playing alto saxophone and later studied at the Berklee College of Music. He played with Roy Haynes and Jack McDuff and then in the quintet of Art Blakey and the Jazz Messengers, together with the trumpeter Terence Blanchard, until 1989.

His own albums from that period include New York Second Line, Black Pearl, The Power of Cool and Indian Blues. In 1991 For Art's Sake appeared, a tribute to Blakey. His work runs through different genres. In 3D Vols. I, II and III he plays smooth jazz and r&b, classic jazz and hip hop, and he also plays with his Electric Band and with The New Sounds of Mardi Gras. In 1999 he became Big Chief of the Congo Square Nation Afro-New Orleans Cultural Group. Later he made Quantum Leap and a first orchestral work, Congo Square Suite, with the Moscow Symphony Orchestra.

Harrison combines bebop, the tradition of New Orleans and hip hop and often records the same song in several styles. He mentored young musicians, including Christian McBride and his nephew, the trumpeter Christian Scott. He is an NEA Jazz Master and played himself in the television series Treme.
artiest/donald-harrison.listen: Listen to a recording of Donald Harrison with his own group and notice how his alto saxophone plays a melody above a rhythm that comes from New Orleans. Can you hear the second line in the drums?

artiest/donna-summer.text:
Donna Summer was born in 1948 as Donna Adrian Gaines in Boston. She sang in church as a child and in 1968 left for Munich, for a part in the German version of the musical Hair. There she met the producers Giorgio Moroder and Pete Bellotte. Together they made disco that increasingly came from machines, and she became known as the Queen of Disco.

The first hit was Love to Love You Baby (1975). Moroder sent a sixteen-minute version to the discotheques. Two years later I Feel Love closed the album I Remember Yesterday (1977). Every track on that record referred to a different era, and this last track was meant to let people hear the future. Apart from the vocals and the bass drum, played by the drummer Keith Forsey, everything comes from a Moog synthesizer with a sequencer. In July 1977 it became her only number 1 hit in England. In 1979 the American number ones Hot Stuff and Bad Girls followed, and in 1983 She Works Hard for the Money.

I Feel Love showed that dance music could be entirely electronic. According to David Bowie, Brian Eno came running into the studio with the record: this was the sound of the future. From the song grew hi-NRG and Italo disco, and later house and techno. The producing trio Stock Aitken Waterman built further in the 1980s on the hi-NRG tempo. Summer died in 2012 in Naples, Florida. A year later she was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.
artiest/donna-summer.listen: In I Feel Love the bass line from the Moog runs like a sequencer pattern that never stops. Listen to how the bass jumps quickly back and forth, while the bass drum, the only truly played drum, hits on every beat and Summer sings high and floating above it.
